summary: Jon Postel's note on the effect of satellite links on the ARPANET. A satellite path adds much more delay without necessarily lowering the data rate. He notes that interactive use with character-at-a-time remote echo is already marginal on the surface network. He asks users to think about how this affects interactive services.

plainLanguage.summary: A satellite route can make a message take longer to arrive, even when it does not lower the transmission rate. This note explains why that delay could make interactive computer use less useful.

subtitle: A warning that satellite paths could add delay to interactive ARPANET sessions.

tldr.problem: Satellite links could lengthen ARPANET paths and increase delay even if they did not change the transmission rate.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel estimates the added path delay and describes effects on remote echo and systems that buffer only a line at a time.
tldr.outcome: The RFC asks the community to discuss buffer sizes, echo techniques, and moving some input processing to the user's system.

sections.title: Path Length and Delay
sections.content:
RFC 346 says a satellite path would affect delay but not necessarily transmission rate. It compares a path of about 44,000 miles through a synchronous-orbit satellite with a worst-case surface path of 3,000 miles, and estimates light travel times for both.

The author uses the change in path length to approximate the change in delay.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer route means more time before a reply arrives. A satellite path can be much longer than a route along the surface.

sections.title: Interactive Echo and Buffers
sections.content:
Postel says interactive servers that echo each typed character remotely were already only marginally useful on the surface ARPANET. Adding a half-second of transmission delay, he argues, could make those systems unusable.

He also discusses systems that buffer one line at a time. Host delays estimated in the RFC could make the time between lines noticeable even with lower-speed output devices.
sections.plainLanguage: When a user waits for each typed character to come back, added delay makes the session feel slow. A small buffer can also leave long gaps between lines.

sections.title: Topics for Further Discussion
sections.content:
The author asks the network community to resume discussion of ways to reduce the effects of large delays. Possible topics include buffer sizes at both ends, echo techniques, and moving some input processing to the user's system.

If echo functions move to the user system, he recommends trying to develop a standard package.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not prescribe one fix. It asks people to discuss several approaches and consider a shared way to handle echo locally.
